lessons.title: Why does the sea go in and out?
lessons.subtitle: The Moon's gentle pull

scenes.title: The sea goes in and out
scenes.narration: Visit a beach in the morning and the sea might be far away. Come back a few hours later, and the water has crept right up the sand. It does this all around the world, every single day. Nobody is pushing it. So what is?

scenes.title: The Moon pulls on the sea
scenes.narration: The answer is the Moon. It is far away, but its gravity still pulls on the Earth. The solid ground hardly moves. But water can flow, so the ocean is pulled into a gentle bulge on the side that faces the Moon.

scenes.title: A bulge on both sides
scenes.narration: There is a second bulge on the far side too! The Moon pulls the nearest water hardest, the Earth a little less, and the farthest water least of all. So the ocean gets stretched out, like a lemon.

draw.s: so the sea stretches, like a lemon

scenes.title: The Earth spins through them
scenes.narration: The bulges stay lined up with the Moon, while the Earth spins around under them once a day. Your beach is carried into a bulge, out of it, into the other bulge, and out again. So most beaches get two high tides and two low tides every day.

scenes.title: The Sun joins in
scenes.narration: The Sun pulls on the sea too, but it is much further away, so its pull is weaker. When the Sun and the Moon line up, their pulls add together and the tides are extra big. When they pull from different sides, the tides are small.

quiz.question: What pulls the sea into a bulge?
quiz.explanation: The Moon's gravity pulls on the ocean, and water is free to flow towards it.

quiz.question: How many high tides do most beaches get each day?
quiz.explanation: There are two bulges, and the spinning Earth carries the beach through both.

quiz.question: When are the tides biggest?
options: When the Sun and Moon line up
When the Moon is hidden by a cloud
quiz.explanation: Their pulls add together, so the bulges get bigger.
